literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It is Halloween, and the books pages have gone suitably eerie, though there is plenty of other good reading alongside the ghosts.

Let me begin with the prizes. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, worth ten thousand pounds, for her book Foretokens. It was announced at the Southbank Centre in London, and The Guardian describes a collection that draws on new parenthood, the death of her father, and her mother's early life in Hong Kong. That mix of the intimate and the inherited sounds like poetry worth seeking out. Elsewhere, the South African novelist Damon Galgut has won the Korean Park Kyung-ni Prize, according to the Korea Herald. Only the headline is available, but it is pleasant news for a Booker-winning writer. And The Conversation has gathered six experts to review the 2026 Booker Prize nominees, arguing that the list is diverse enough to suit all sorts of readers. If you like to see a prize list discussed with some critical substance, that is the one to open.

Now to voices, which I suspect is where you will linger. The Guardian reviews Attention Seeking Behaviour, a debut by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo, shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize. Its narrator shares the author's name and confesses, from the start, that she is a liar. The reviewer sets it beside Lolita and Atonement, which tells you the territory: memory, justice, and how far we can trust anyone who tells us their own story. It sounds like a lovely thing to put in front of première students who are learning to distrust a charming narrator.

Also in The Guardian, there is an interview with Helen Garner, the Australian author of unsparing fiction and true crime. She talks about surviving three marriages, about being called a "rotten feminist", and about finding global recognition five decades into her career. Her line that being hated is "very bracing" gives you a good sense of the voice: frank, self-possessed, not remotely anxious to be liked.

Philippa Gregory, meanwhile, tells The Guardian that she read one hundred of the eighteenth century's most popular novels, and calls it the perfect author's apprenticeship. She also admits that she came to Dickens rather late, and talks about Molly Keane and Elizabeth Goudge, and about why history belongs in fiction. Given how much you value novels that teach the past better than a textbook, her case for it is worth a few minutes.

Staying with writers' lives, The Guardian's monthly "what we're reading" round-up has Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and readers sharing their October favourites. One pick is James Bailey's biography of Muriel Spark, praised for being both detailed and readable. Spark is a writer with a famously sharp narrative voice, so a biography that keeps pace with her sounds promising. The Guardian also has a roundup of recent translated fiction. It features Barbi Marković's Minihorror, described as eccentric, fantastical micro-fictions, along with new books by Pol Guasch, Helle Helle and Hamid Ismailov. If you want a strong voice from outside English, this is a handy map.

Now for the spookier corner. Literary Hub offers ten poems to read this Halloween, deliberately by poets not usually associated with horror, so it moves beyond the familiar trio of Poe, Dickinson and Shelley. Atmospheric verse suits an evening like this one, and it may give you a few unexpected poems to share in class. The Guardian reviews a new audio production of Bram Stoker's Dracula, directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, with a starry cast that includes Jonathan Bailey. The reviewer admires its streamlined storytelling and its immersive, nightmarish sound design, and calls it cinematic horror. That sounds well suited to a dark autumn evening in the mountains.

Looking a little further ahead, The Booker Prizes site has a reading list of five books by Mexican authors, prompted by Day of the Dead, which falls on Monday, the second of November. It is the kind of list that opens a culture to the reader without asking for any prior knowledge, which I know you appreciate.

Finally, a few pieces about form, image and music. Literary Hub asks why serial fiction is having a moment, and it starts with Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, published in nineteen instalments from eighteen thirty-six. The piece is brief, but it touches on how the shape of publication shapes both stories and reading habits, which is a rather nice thing to hold in mind when you teach a Victorian novel. Literary Hub also picks the ten best book covers of October, chosen for their colour, texture and wit. It is a light, visual read, and a pleasing reminder of how image and text meet before you have read a word.

On the musical side, The Paris Review Daily has a short piece on the cellist Alisa Weilerstein, opening with a playful image of the cello in flight. It is brief, but it has that lyrical register you enjoy. And Local News Matters, in its Hooked on Books series, has a piece on George Saunders moving from page to stage in an opera style. I only have the headline, so I cannot tell you more, but the idea of Saunders's voice meeting music is intriguing enough on its own.

That is your literary round-up for today. Enjoy the poems and the ghosts, Yamuna, and I hope the evening is gently spooky.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It is Halloween, and the books pages have obliged with a little darkness, a good deal of fine voices, and a handful of prizes to talk about over coffee.

Let me begin with the season. The Guardian has reviewed a new audiobook of Bram Stoker's Dracula, and it sounds like a treat for the evening. It is directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, with a starry cast that includes Jonathan Bailey. The reviewer calls it cinematic horror, praising a streamlined version of the story and a sound design that is immersive and properly nightmarish. Dracula is, of course, a novel built from voices: letters, diaries, journal entries, each narrator seeing only a fragment. So hearing it performed by a full cast feels less like an adaptation than a return to how the book is put together. If you have a dark evening and a good pair of headphones, it may be worth a listen.

On the poetry side, Literary Hub has a list called Something Wicked This Way Comes, ten poems to read this Halloween. What I like about it is the premise. It steps beyond the usual suspects, Poe, Dickinson and Shelley, and instead chooses eerie poems by poets who are not generally thought of as writers of horror. That is often where the best unease lives: a poet known for tenderness or for clear daylight observation suddenly lets a shadow into the room. It is the sort of list that would work well read aloud, one poem at a time, with the lamp turned low. And it might even be a small gift for a classroom, a way of showing pupils that atmosphere is made of word choice and rhythm rather than of ghosts.

Staying with the turn of the calendar, the Booker Prizes site has put together a Day of the Dead reading list of five books by Mexican authors. Day of the Dead falls on the second of November, so the timing is neat. I mention it because it is the kind of list you enjoy: novels that open a culture to the reader without asking them to arrive already knowing it. The feast, with its mix of mourning and celebration, has always sat close to literature's oldest concerns, so a reading list built around it feels like a natural way in.

Now to the voices, which I suspect are the heart of today's briefing.

The Guardian reviews Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo, a debut that has been shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize. The narrator shares the author's name, and she begins by confessing that she is a liar. You can see at once why this is catnip for a reader of unreliable narrators. The review calls it a slippery liar's tale, and sets it alongside Lolita and Atonement, two books in which the storyteller's control over the truth is the whole drama. The themes it is said to explore are memory, justice and truth: what we owe to the people we tell stories about, and what happens when the teller cannot be trusted. A narrator who confesses first, and then keeps you guessing about what the confession is worth, is a delicious trap. It might even be useful for your older pupils, who always find it thrilling to be told, in the very first pages, that they should not believe what they are about to read.

From a liar to a very frank speaker. The Guardian also has an interview with Helen Garner, the Australian writer of unsparing fiction and true crime. The headline gives you her tone: being hated, she says, is very bracing. She talks about surviving three marriages, and about being called a rotten feminist, and about finding global recognition five decades into her career. There is something wonderfully self-possessed in all of that. Garner has built a body of work on looking hard at things other people prefer to look away from, and it sounds as though the interview carries that same candour. If you like a memorable narrator, and I know you do, a writer whose own speaking voice is this direct is a pleasure to meet.

Then there is Philippa Gregory, who is also in The Guardian, and whose piece speaks directly to your taste for history learned through fiction. She describes reading a hundred of the eighteenth century's most popular novels, and calls it the perfect apprenticeship for an author. I find that rather charming: not the great canonical books, but the popular ones, the bestsellers of their day, read in bulk until she understood how stories were being told and what readers wanted. She also recalls coming to Dickens late, which is a reassuring confession from a writer of her standing. And she talks about Molly Keane and Elizabeth Goudge, and makes the case for why history belongs in fiction. For anyone who has ever argued that a novel can teach the texture of a period better than a textbook, it is a pleasing ally.

A final note on reading lives. The Guardian's monthly round-up, What we're reading, has Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and a number of readers sharing what they enjoyed in October. One pick stands out: James Bailey's biography of Muriel Spark, praised for its detail and its readability. Spark is a writer of such economy and mischief that a good biography of her feels like a promise, and the fact that it is described as readable suggests it keeps up with its subject.

Let me turn to prizes, because three of them have been in the news.

The warmest story is in poetry. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, for her book Foretokens. The Guardian reports that the book is about new parenthood, the death of her father, and her mother's early life in Hong Kong. It was announced at London's Southbank Centre, and the prize carries ten thousand pounds. What strikes me is how much sits inside that description: the arrival of a child, the loss of a parent, and a mother's earlier life in another place, all held in the one collection. That layering of generations feels like exactly what poetry does well, and I would be curious to hear how the language handles it.

Then, the Booker Prize. The Conversation has gathered six experts to review the nominees for the twenty twenty-six prize, arguing that the list is diverse enough to inspire all sorts of readers. I only have the framing and not the individual verdicts, but the idea of six different critics each taking a book, rather than one voice judging the whole, is appealing. It gives a sense of the list as a range of possible reading lives instead of a single league table. If you are looking for a way into this year's contenders, that may be a good place to begin.

And from further afield, the South African novelist Damon Galgut, a Booker winner, has been awarded the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award. The report from the Korea Herald is only a headline, so I cannot tell you more about the citation, but it is nice to see a writer recognised across borders, in a prize named for a Korean author.

That brings me neatly to writing from beyond English. The Guardian has a review roundup of recent translated fiction, and it is a good one for finding a strong new voice. It covers Minihorror by Barbi Marković, described as eccentric, fantastical micro-fictions, which pairs rather well with today's Halloween mood. It also covers new books by Pol Guasch, Helle Helle and Hamid Ismailov. The roundup format is useful here: a few lines on each writer, enough to tell you whether a particular voice is going to suit you, and a chance to follow up on whichever sounds most distinctive. Micro-fictions in particular can be a lovely thing to bring to a classroom, because you can read an entire story in a couple of minutes and then spend the rest of the lesson talking about how it was done.

Finally, a few pieces about the shape and sound of storytelling itself.

Literary Hub asks why serial fiction is having a moment. The piece begins with Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, which appeared in nineteen instalments from eighteen thirty-six. I only have the opening to go on, but it is a good question to ask. Serial publication shaped how Dickens plotted, how he built suspense, how readers talked among themselves between episodes, and it is intriguing to think that our habits of reading in small, regular pieces are coming round again. You could imagine it as a lovely way to introduce first-year pupils to a Victorian novel: one instalment at a time, with a cliffhanger.

From the page to the stage: Local News Matters, in its Hooked on Books series, has a piece on George Saunders wandering from page to stage in an opera style. I should be honest that I only have the headline, so I cannot say what exactly is being staged. But for a reader who loves Saunders' prose and loves music, the pairing alone is intriguing, since his writing has such a distinct musical ear, with its looping, tender, comic rhythms.

There is also a short piece in The Paris Review Daily about the cellist Alisa Weilerstein. It opens with a playful image of the cello in flight. Again, it is brief, but the opening promises that lyrical register you tend to enjoy, and it sits happily at the border between writing and music.

And last, a purely visual pleasure: Literary Hub has chosen the ten best book covers of October, picked for their colour stories, textures and wit. It is a light thing, but a pleasing one, and it touches on that old question of how an image prepares us for the words inside it. If you enjoy the conversation between painting and literature, a scroll through a month of covers is a small and cheerful way to indulge it.

That is all for this morning, Yamuna; I hope your Halloween reading is deliciously unsettling, and that the lamp stays low and the tea stays hot.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the thirty-first of October, and this morning's art news has a pleasing mix of local doors to push open, a few stories where paintings and books meet, and some remarkable lives behind the work.

Let's begin at home. This afternoon at four thirty, the Musée de Grenoble is running its flash visits of the collection. They're short, open to everyone, and an easy way to spend half an hour with the museum without planning a whole outing. And tomorrow, Sunday the first of November, evous reminds us that museums in Grenoble offer free admission, the Musée de Grenoble among them. If the weather turns grey over the Grésivaudan, that sounds like a good day to wander through galleries. Also in the city, Unidivers tells us the Mois de la Photo has chosen the theme of hors-champ, the off-frame, as its central idea. There are no dates or venues in the piece I have, but it's a lovely notion: what lies just beyond the edge of a picture, and what a photograph chooses not to show. It might even make a good prompt for your première students thinking about what a narrator leaves out.

Lyon next, for when you fancy a trip. Le Petit Bulletin reviews the eighteenth Lyon Biennale, themed around passage, and calls it a very beautiful one. It praises a strong focus on Oceanian artists, and the more intimate works, particularly at the Musée d'art contemporain. The same publication points to the Musée des Confluences, where an exhibition called Animal culte traces our relationships with animals across time and cultures, from sacred animal icons and companions to the mass decline of species. The title carries a gentle reproach, something like "our friends, whom we harm". And jds.fr lists a Lyon exhibition titled Institut d'art de Chicago, le musée-monde, presenting work linked to the Art Institute of Chicago. I've no further detail beyond the title, but it's worth a look at the dates and times if you're heading that way.

Now for the meeting of art and literature, which I suspect is your favourite corner. The Guardian's week in art highlights an exhibition at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge on late Victorian art and politics, with William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites, running until the third of May. Morris, of course, was a designer, a poet and a writer all at once, so the show sits very comfortably between painting and the page. On BBC Radio 4's Front Row, the critics review Nina Raine's six-hour adaptation of Middlemarch for the Royal Shakespeare Company, and ask how the stage version measures up against George Eliot's novel. The same programme covers the British Library's exhibition on Agatha Christie, marking fifty years since her death. Six hours of Middlemarch is a bold undertaking, and I rather love that someone thought the novel deserved that much room.

Further afield in France, in La Clayette, in Saône-et-Loire, the collégiens' art gallery is showing an exhibition of artists' books. The report is short and gives no dates, but it's a nice idea: books that are works of art in themselves, made by young people. And from Beaux Arts Magazine comes a story that sends you back to a canvas you may think you know. Scientists say they have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. I'd treat the word "may" with care, but it's a charming invitation to look up, and then look again at those swirling stars.

Several pieces today are about the people behind the pictures. In Paris, the Musée Maillol is showing an exhibition on Dina Vierny, who was the sculptor Maillol's muse, but also a member of the Resistance and a collector. Jds.fr presents it as a story that joins an artist's work to wartime history, which is exactly the sort of biography that reads like a novel. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on a donation of amateur photographs entering a museum, with subjects ranging from the love story of an anonymous couple to a picture connected with Alfred Dreyfus. The article doesn't name the museum, so I can't tell you whether it's close to home, but I like the thought of ordinary snapshots turning, quietly, into history. And The Guardian profiles the Iranian-born artist Hoda Afshar. She grew up under Iran's morality police, and that experience shapes work that looks for humanity inside inhumane systems. "I don't take freedom of speech for granted," she says, which is a line worth sitting with.

Lastly, two pleasures for the ear and the eye. The Guardian reviews William Kentridge's Oh to Believe in Another World, an hour-long collage animation staged in Baku, with a live orchestra playing Shostakovich's Tenth Symphony. The reviewer calls it an amazing animated ballet of black comic pain, blending puppetry, dance and humour around grief and idealism. It sounds like a perfect meeting of your tastes in music, movement and inventive images. And to finish on something warmer, the National Gallery has posted a short video in which the curators Christopher Riopelle and Chiara Di Stefano talk about Renoir's paintings of friends, family and lovers, linked to its Renoir and Love exhibition. Renoir, they say, was absolutely fascinated by love, and the clip is a brief, easy way into that gentler side of him.

Enjoy the weekend, Yamuna, and may tomorrow's free museums be as bright as the stars in Van Gogh's sky.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Saturday the thirty-first of October, and today's art news runs from a Grenoble afternoon visit to a ballet in Baku, with a few detours through novels, stars and snapshots along the way.

Let me begin close to home, because there's something you could do this very afternoon. At the Musée de Grenoble, at half past four, there are flash visits of the collection. They're short, open to everyone, and meant as an easy way in, a handful of works looked at properly rather than a whole museum tackled at once. If the weather in the valley turns grey, as it often does at the end of October, it's a pleasant way to spend an hour.

And if this afternoon doesn't work, tomorrow might. The site evous reports that on Sunday the first of November, museums in Grenoble are offering free admission, the Musée de Grenoble among them. It's a bank-holiday weekend, so I'd expect it to be lively, but free entry is a good excuse to go back to a room you love, or to wander into one you've never quite got round to. I'd suggest checking the opening hours of whichever museum you choose before setting out.

Still in Grenoble, there's news from the Mois de la Photo. Unidivers reports that this edition puts the idea of hors-champ at the centre, the off-frame, everything that lies just beyond the edge of the picture. The piece I've seen doesn't give dates or venues, so I can't tell you where to go, but I do like the theme. A photograph is as much about what it leaves out as what it shows, and that's a rather literary idea too, isn't it? Any good narrator knows that what goes unsaid carries as much weight as what's said. It might even make a nice prompt for a class on point of view.

That thought leads neatly to a story from Le Dauphiné Libéré. A donation of amateur photographs is entering a museum, and the pictures range from the love story of an anonymous couple to an image connected with Alfred Dreyfus. The report doesn't name the museum, so I can't promise a local link. But the idea is lovely: ordinary snapshots, taken by people who never expected to be remembered, become part of history once an institution decides they matter. It's the same pleasure as a good historical novel, where the large events are seen through very small, very human lives.

Now to Lyon, which has three things worth knowing about, and which might make a good day out if the museums in Grenoble are crowded tomorrow.

First, the Lyon Biennale. Le Petit Bulletin has reviewed the eighteenth edition, which takes passage as its theme, and the verdict is warm: a very beautiful passage, to borrow the headline's pun. The reviewer praises a strong focus on Oceanian artists, and also the more intimate works, especially those at the Musée d'art contemporain. It sounds like a biennale that rewards slow looking rather than shouting for attention, and that's often the best sort. If you're planning a trip, the review sounds like a useful guide for deciding where to begin.

Second, also from Le Petit Bulletin, an exhibition at the Musée des Confluences called Animal culte, with the subtitle, roughly, our pals that we damage. It traces the relationship between humans and animals across time and across cultures. There are animal icons, animal companions, and then the darker thread of mass animal decline. It sounds like the kind of show where anthropology, history and museum display all work together, and where the tone moves from affection to uncomfortable reflection. For someone who likes learning history through stories, the long, shared story of people and animals seems a rich one.

Third, jds.fr lists an exhibition in Lyon titled Institut d'art de Chicago: le musée-monde, the Art Institute of Chicago as a world museum. I only have the title, no details of what's on show, so I can't tell you which paintings have travelled. But a major international museum presenting its collection in Lyon is worth keeping an eye on, and the listing gives dates, opening hours and prices if you want to look.

Let me turn now to the places where art and literature meet, which I suspect is where you'll linger longest.

Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists believe they've identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. I only have the headline claim, not the method, so I won't pretend to explain how they did it. But the idea is irresistible: that the swirling heavens over that village might correspond to a real sky seen on a real night. It invites you to look at the canvas again and ask what a painter does with what he sees. Is it observation, memory, feeling? That's a question every writer faces too, and it would sit well alongside any description of a night sky in a poem or a novel.

On the stage side, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has an episode reviewing Nina Raine's six-hour adaptation of Middlemarch for the Royal Shakespeare Company. Six hours! The review asks how the stage version compares with the novel, which is a question worth asking of any adaptation, and of this novel especially, with its huge cast of provincial lives and its famously patient, wise narrator. How do you stage a narrator's voice? I'd be curious to hear whether the production finds a way. The same programme also covers the British Library's exhibition on Agatha Christie, marking fifty years since her death. For a lover of thrillers, that one has an obvious pull, and it's a reminder of how a writer can become a whole world, a method and a mood, not just a shelf of books.

Also on the literary side, there's a smaller story from La Renaissance Hebdo. At La Clayette, in Saône-et-Loire, the collégiens' art gallery is showing an exhibition of artists' books. It's a short piece with no dates, and La Clayette is a good way from Les Adrets, so it's not a day trip. But I like it for what it shows: schoolchildren making books that are also works of art, where the page, the image and the object all count. It might spark an idea for a project with your own pupils.

And from The Guardian's week in art, a note on the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, which is showing an exhibition on late Victorian art and politics, with William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites, until the third of May. The Guardian's roundup also mentions big hair, hence the headline, as well as seventeen standout works in Orkney and some night frights in Derry, but the Fitzwilliam show is the one that ties painting most closely to writing and design. Morris and the pre-Raphaelites are a gift for anyone who loves the links between pictures and poems, and the fact that the show frames them politically should make it richer. With the end date in May, there's plenty of time if a trip to England is on the cards.

Now to the people behind the work, which is where several of today's stories end up.

Start with Dina Vierny. jds.fr writes about an exhibition at the Musée Maillol in Paris that presents her as muse, Resistance member and collector. Three roles in one life: the model who posed for Maillol, the woman who acted in wartime, and the person who later gathered art. It's a biography that cuts across sculpture and history, and it's the sort of life that deserves a novel. If you're in Paris, it sounds like a story-driven show rather than a purely aesthetic one.

Then Hoda Afshar. The Guardian profiles the Iranian-born artist, whose youth under Iran's morality police shapes work that finds humanity inside inhumane systems. The headline calls her work beautiful and shocking, and quotes her saying she doesn't take freedom of speech for granted. What strikes me is the emphasis on personal testimony and visual storytelling. She's an artist who speaks from experience, and in that sense she's a narrator as much as a photographer or image-maker. It's a thoughtful read if you're interested in how a first-person voice can be carried through pictures.

For something altogether warmer, there's a short video from the National Gallery in London. Curators Christopher Riopelle and Chiara Di Stefano talk about Renoir's paintings of friends, family and lovers, in connection with the exhibition Renoir and Love. As the title of the clip puts it, Renoir was absolutely fascinated by love. It's brief, just a few minutes, and a friendly way into the more intimate side of his work, the painter of the people he cared about rather than the grand subject.

And finally, the most spectacular piece of the day, from The Guardian. William Kentridge's Oh to Believe in Another World is an hour-long collage animation staged in Baku, with a live orchestra playing Shostakovich's Tenth Symphony. The reviewer calls it an amazing animated ballet of black comic pain. It blends puppetry, dance and humour, circling around grief and idealism. I can't think of a better description of something that would suit you: music, movement and inventive visual art, with a streak of dark comedy running through the sorrow. The review is worth reading even if you can't see the production, if only to enjoy how the critic describes the mixture of laughter and loss.

So there's the day: a flash visit this afternoon, free museums tomorrow, a Lyon trip to think about, and plenty of stories behind the pictures to read on the sofa when the evening draws in.

Enjoy your Saturday, Yamuna, and may your Sunday be full of open doors.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's the last day of October, and the past two days have brought one sad piece of news and a good handful of stage and page links for your 2027 and oral texts.

The sad news first. The Guardian reports the death of Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of eighty-six, describing him as a Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian. Several other outlets have followed with tributes, and between them they share one theme, which is useful for a Shakespeare teacher. CP24 offers a profile of his life, nineteen forty to twenty twenty-six, tracing the path from Shakespearean actor to starship captain. The Irish News argues that Shakespeare was his first love, before Star Trek made him famous, and presents him as an actor whose classical training shaped his whole career. Everything Zoomer takes a similar line under the headline about his final bow, moving from Shakespeare to Star Trek, and describes a warm profile of a stage actor. PBS has also posted a tribute on its Great Performances news page. The text there is thin, but it points towards his stage and screen work, and it may be a good place to look for performance recordings to use with students. The pieces are brief, so I wouldn't build a lesson on them alone. But they offer a gentle way into a conversation with seconde or première about what classical training does for an actor, and why a voice trained on Shakespeare can carry into a very different world. That could sit nicely beside Hamlet or Twelfth Night.

Speaking of which, there is some news on staging. For Twelfth Night, Everything Theatre has published a review of a production at the Crucible Theatre. I only have the fact of the review, not its content, so I can't tell you what the critic made of it. But a critical account of a staging is always handy for helping students see that a play is an interpretation as well as a text. Alongside it, the Taunton Daily Gazette reports a reimagining of Twelfth Night as a 1960s jazz club. That is all I have, a headline, but it is an appealing premise for a discussion of adaptation. You might ask students what a jazz club setting could do for the play's music, disguise and lovesickness, and what it might lose.

For Hamlet, there is a new staging at the Barbican in London, titled Hamlet Hail to the Thief. West End Theatre has released first-look images, and Theatre Weekly has published behind-the-scenes photographs as previews begin. I don't have descriptions of what the images show, so I can't say how the production looks. But production photographs are a quick, visual way into a staging discussion with a class, particularly for students who find the play's long speeches hard to picture. Once you've seen them, you will know whether they are worth bringing into a lesson.

Two more of the 2027 texts have local productions in the news. Swansea Bay News carries a reviewer's verdict on Swansea Little Theatre's Under Milk Wood at the Dylan Thomas Theatre. The article poses the question of whether it is worth seeing, and I can't tell you the answer, but the review may help you judge how the staging handles a play written so much for the ear. And in Northwich, the Northwich Guardian reports that the town's theatre will stage the wartime comedy Jack Absolute Flies Again from this November. The title suggests a link to Jack Absolute, a character from Sheridan's The Rivals, though the information I have doesn't spell out the connection, so I'd treat that as a hint rather than a certainty. If it does hold, it would make a neat example of a later work borrowing a character from an older comedy.

Now to the oral themes list, where Orwell is having something of a moment. The Herald and News carries an op-ed arguing that 1984 was a warning, not an instruction manual. It could be a handy prompt for a class discussion on what Orwell meant the novel to do, and whether readers sometimes mistake a warning for a blueprint. Searchlight Magazine, meanwhile, reviews Orwell: the Road to 1984, a play by Guy Smith about the path leading to the novel. I have no further details, but the idea of how a book came to be written is a good source of context for students. Taken together, the two pieces give you a before and an after: how the novel was reached, and how it is read today.

There is also an Observer opinion piece, headlined that Gilead is not fiction and is coming for all women again today. I only have the headline. It concerns Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale, and it is plainly politically charged, so I would use it with care, if at all. If you do, it might work best as an example of how readers use a novel to talk about the present, with students invited to weigh that critically rather than simply accept it.

Finally, a lovely teaching link for Never Let Me Go. NPR has an interview with Kazuo Ishiguro in which he discusses Klara and the Sun and his approach to writing novels about the future. I don't have the details of what he says, but it is a promising piece for students preparing the oral. Hearing an author talk about how he imagines the future may help them see Never Let Me Go as a novel about a world that is close to ours, rather than far away.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope the weekend gives you time for a good book and a warm drink.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's the last day of October, and today's corner is rather theatrical: a farewell to a great Shakespearean, several stagings of your 2027 texts, and a few useful pieces for the oral list.

Let me begin with the sad news, which dominated the last two days. The Guardian reports the death of Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of eighty-six, describing him as a Star Trek actor and an acclaimed thespian. Of the obituaries I've seen, it's the most authoritative, and it comes from a paper with a long tradition of taking the stage seriously. Several other outlets have run tributes, and they share a theme that may interest you as a teacher of Shakespeare: the arc from the classical stage to the starship.

CP24 has a profile marking his life, nineteen forty to twenty twenty-six, tracing his path from Shakespearean actor to starship captain. I should be honest that the text is brief, so it's more an outline than a deep portrait. The Irish News goes a step further with a feature arguing that Shakespeare was his first love, before Star Trek made him famous. It offers a human angle on an actor whose classical training shaped his career, and that makes it a gentler way into a lesson on Shakespearean performance than a technical essay would be. Everything Zoomer has a similar piece, headed "From Shakespeare to Star Trek, the Actor Takes His Final Bow". It's a warm profile of a stage actor, with a Shakespearean angle that could sit comfortably beside a lesson on Hamlet or Twelfth Night.

Finally, PBS has published an In Memoriam tribute on its Great Performances news page. The text I have is thin, but it points to his stage and screen work, and it may be a useful signpost if you want to look for performance recordings to show students. I can't say which recordings it names, so it's worth a look yourself before planning anything. If you did want to build a short classroom moment around him, the common thread in these pieces would serve well: an actor who treated Shakespeare as a foundation rather than a footnote. You could ask première students what it means for an actor to be trained in classical text, and how that might show in the way a speech is spoken.

Now to the stage, and to Twelfth Night, which is on the session twenty twenty-seven list. Two items this week. Everything Theatre has published a review of a production at the Crucible Theatre. I only have the fact of the review, not its verdict, so I can't tell you whether the staging is bold or traditional. A critical account of a production is nonetheless a good classroom object. Reading a review alongside the text teaches students to separate what Shakespeare wrote from what a director decided, which is a real skill for the written paper.

The second Twelfth Night item is from the Taunton Daily Gazette, which reports a reimagining of the play as a 1960s jazz club. Again, all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you how the idea is carried through. But the premise is lovely for teaching adaptation. You might ask students why a jazz club suits this play. Is it the music, since the comedy opens with an appetite for music? Is it the atmosphere of disguise and night-time licence? Let them argue for or against the transposition before they find out how the production handled it. For seconde, it could be a gentle way into the idea that a play can be moved to another era without losing its heart. For terminale students, it opens a more critical question: when does an updated setting illuminate a text, and when does it simply decorate it?

Next, Hamlet, also on the twenty twenty-seven programme. Two outlets have covered a new staging at the Barbican in London, titled Hamlet Hail to the Thief. West End Theatre has released first-look images, and Theatre Weekly has published behind-the-scenes photography as previews begin. The pieces are mostly visual, so I can't describe the concept or the casting, and I won't guess. What I can say is that production photographs are a wonderfully quick teaching resource. Put two or three images on the board and ask students what the costume, the lighting and the grouping of figures suggest about the world of the play, before you tell them anything else. It trains the same close attention you'd ask of a passage of text, but through the eye. And given your love of the links between painting and literature, photographs of a staging fit naturally with that habit of reading an image as carefully as a page. Previews have only just begun, so reviews should follow in the coming weeks, and I'll flag them when they do.

From Shakespeare to Wales, and Under Milk Wood, which is on the twenty twenty-seven list. Swansea Bay News has a reviewer's verdict on Swansea Little Theatre's production at the Dylan Thomas Theatre, framed as a question: is it worth seeing? The text I have doesn't give the answer, so you'll need to read it for yourself. But it's a useful kind of source for you, because Under Milk Wood is a play for voices, and a review of a local staging can help you judge how a production handles that. It may also be a handy example for students of how a local company approaches a famous text, and a reminder that these works are alive on small stages as well as great ones.

A smaller item, but one with a pleasing link to the programme. The Northwich Guardian reports that the town's theatre will stage a wartime comedy, Jack Absolute Flies Again, from November. The title suggests that it draws on Jack Absolute, who is a character in Sheridan's The Rivals, also on the twenty twenty-seven list. I can't confirm anything further about the play from what I have, so treat the connection as a promising hint rather than established fact. If it holds, it's a nice example of a later writer borrowing a name and a type from an eighteenth-century comedy and carrying it into a new setting. That could make a short, playful exercise in the classroom: what does it mean to take a character out of one century and place him in another, and what does the audience bring with them when they recognise the name?

Now to the oral themes list, where there are four items, and a common thread of novels that read as warnings.

The most directly useful for you is an NPR interview with Kazuo Ishiguro, in which he discusses Klara and the Sun and his approach to writing novels about the future. Never Let Me Go is on your oral list, so this is a strong teaching link. I only have the outline of the interview, not the detail of what he says, but the subject itself is rich. A novelist reflecting on how he imagines the future is just what students need when they ask why an author would set a story in a world that doesn't exist. You could pair listening to the interview with a few pages of Never Let Me Go and ask: what is the novel doing with the future that a history book or a news report could not? It's an audio source too, which makes it easy to use in class.

Orwell's 1984 appears twice. The Herald and News carries an op-ed arguing that 1984 was a warning, not an instruction manual. It's a crisp, memorable line, and it makes a good discussion prompt about the purpose of the novel. Students can be asked whether a book can be a warning if people misread it, and what, in the text, tells us what Orwell intended. The second is a theatre review in Searchlight Magazine of Orwell: the Road to 1984, by Guy Smith, a play about the path leading to Orwell's novel. I only have the framing, not the review's contents, but a play about how the book came to be written suggests useful context for teaching it. Read together, the two pieces offer a pleasing pairing: one asks what the novel is for, the other asks where it came from. That is the sort of question that helps students move from summary to analysis in an oral.

The last item needs more care. The Observer has an opinion piece headed, "Gilead is not fiction. It is coming for all women again today." The text I've been given is only that headline. Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale is on the oral list, so it could support class discussion, but it is politically charged, and I'd suggest you use it with care. If you do, one way would be to treat it as an example of a writer using a novel as a lens on current events, and to ask students to examine the rhetoric of the headline itself. What is it claiming, and what does it assume? That keeps the focus on language and argument, which is where your lessons are strongest, rather than on taking a side. Of course, you know your classes far better than I do, and you may well decide to leave it on the shelf.

To pull the threads together: if you want something for next week, I'd suggest the Ishiguro interview for the oral, and a gallery of Hamlet production photographs for a première lesson on staging. The Twelfth Night jazz club idea is a nice short exercise in adaptation, and the Patrick Stewart tributes give you a gentle, human way into why classical training matters to a performer.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna. I hope your Saturday has a little theatre in it, and perhaps a quiet walk in the Belledonne autumn light.

Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a lot of art, language and quiet kindness in it, with a few lovely things for a Saturday morning in Les Adrets.

Let me begin with the past, which turns up in several surprising places. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. It's a lovely meeting of astronomy and painting, and it invites you to look again at that swirling canvas, perhaps with your première class, and ask what he saw and what he invented.

Staying with objects and their stories, Good News Network reports that researchers have replicated Roman dichroic glass, the kind that changes colour depending on the light, for the first time in around sixteen hundred years. Ancient craft and modern materials science, working together to bring back something a Roman maker once held up to the sun.

And The Guardian reports on a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse, the scientist who was lost on Louis the Sixteenth's round-the-world voyage of seventeen eighty-five. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give a personal account of the expedition. It reads rather like the opening of a novel, a mystery of the sea told through the voice of a man in love.

Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells of a donation of amateur photographs entering a museum. The subjects range from the love story of an anonymous couple to a picture connected with Alfred Dreyfus. The text doesn't name the museum, so I can't say whether it's near you, but I like the idea of ordinary snapshots slowly becoming history, one unknown face at a time.

Now to the mind and to language. Good News Network reports new research suggesting that the expertise needed to identify birds helps preserve neuroplasticity, and may slow cognitive decline in ageing. The piece opens with Emily Dickinson's line about hope being the thing with feathers, which feels about right. Perhaps a good excuse for a walk with binoculars along the Grésivaudan. And speaking of walking, Upworthy has a short piece on a linguist showing how English expressions such as "by the way" and "of course" reveal a hidden metaphor: that thinking is walking. The article is slight, but it might make a charming starter for a lesson. Words like "way" and "course" are really paths, and we've been strolling along them all our lives without noticing.

On the stage and the screen, Royal Ballet and Opera has a video of principal dancer Yasmine Naghdi talking about returning to rehearsals, and to the Main Stage, as Manon after maternity leave. Manon runs at the Royal Opera House until the twenty-fifth of November, and the cinema broadcast is still showing until Tuesday the third of November, so there's a small window if you'd like to see it on a big screen.

Good News Network also has a short documentary called Panther Pat, about Pat Palinkas. She was an elementary school teacher who, in nineteen seventy, became the first woman to play professional football, taking the field for the Orlando Panthers. She's a nearly forgotten figure with a strong story, and a teacher at that, which you might enjoy.

In the world of books, The Guardian reports that Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, with Foretokens. The book moves between new parenthood, her father's death and her mother's early life in Hong Kong. The prize was announced at London's Southbank Centre and carries ten thousand pounds. It sounds like poetry in which the personal and the historical share a single breath. Also, the Korea Herald reports that the South African novelist Damon Galgut has won the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award. I only have the headline, but it is welcome recognition for a Booker-winning writer.

And now three stories of people being noticed, which I think are the heart of today. Good News Network tells of He Ziqi, now a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence, who was admitted to a prestigious university partly because of a strawberry farmer. The farmer's phone number had appeared, without his knowing, on a middle-school English exam. He now uses the calls he gets to inspire others. It's a very warm story, and a gentle comedy about how far a small thing can travel.

Also from Good News Network, a new school in Texas has been named for Marilyn Hampton, a longtime custodian known to everyone as Miss Marilyn. The honour moved her deeply, and there's a video of her reaction. It's a pleasing correction to the way we usually decide whose names go on buildings.

And The Optimist Daily's podcast for the thirtieth of October features Vivian Ho, a teenager who built a supply network where families can request goods without filling in any forms. She also sends handmade crafts reflecting each family's cultural background, which is a lovely touch of dignity. The same episode touches on a wildlife deal in Kenya and on energy security and electric vehicles, if you want to listen further.

Finally, two small notes from history. Good News Network reminds us that today is the anniversary of the birth of the British-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, seventy-six years ago. The piece recalls her knighthood, and her London firm, which continues to innovate. And from yesterday's entry, on the thirtieth of October nineteen seventy-three, the Bosporus Bridge was completed, linking mainland Europe with Anatolia for the first time, with its steel towers and inclined hangers carrying a continent across the water.

I hope something in there keeps you company today, perhaps even a bird.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's the last day of October, and the past couple of days have brought a pleasingly bookish and artful handful of good news: old paintings, old letters, new prizes, and a few small acts of kindness.

Let me begin with the stories that ask us to look again at things we thought we knew. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. The wording is careful, "may have inspired", and I think that's rather lovely, because it keeps a little mystery alive. But the idea is a delight: that the swirling, restless heavens of one of the most reproduced paintings in the world might be tied to a real sky, one that astronomy can actually pin down. It's the kind of link between a canvas and a science that invites you back to the picture with fresh eyes. If you ever want to set a poem about stars beside the painting for your première students, this could be a charming way in, a reminder that imagination and observation are not opposites.

Staying with things we can look at in a new light, quite literally, there's a story from Good News Network about Roman glass. Researchers have replicated Roman dichroic glass, the kind that changes colour depending on the light, after roughly sixteen hundred years. Think of that for a moment. A craft that vanished from knowledge has been recovered, and it took modern materials science to understand what ancient hands were doing. A glass that shifts from one colour to another as the light moves seems almost made for a poet, and it's a fine meeting of ancient skill, chemistry and the history of objects. It says something gentle, too, about how much human ingenuity can be lost and then, with patience, found again.

And from nearer to home in spirit, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells of a donation of amateur photographs that is entering a museum. The subjects range from the story of an anonymous couple in love, people whose names we apparently don't know, to a picture connected with Alfred Dreyfus. The text doesn't name the museum, so I can't tell you whether it's somewhere you could visit on a weekend, but the idea is a good one. Ordinary snapshots, taken by people who never imagined they were making history, become part of the record. It's the same instinct that makes novels teach history so well: the large events are seen through the small, human, unnamed lives. Those unknown lovers, I suspect, may be more affecting than a great many famous faces.

That brings me to a handful of stories from the past that read like fiction. The Guardian reports on a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse, the scientist who was lost on Louis XVI's round-the-world voyage of seventeen eighty-five. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give a personal account of the expedition. So here is a famous maritime mystery, the ship that sailed out and never came home, suddenly given a voice: not the voice of an official report, but of a man in love, writing to someone he cared about. You couldn't ask for a better narrator, or a better opening for a novel. The Guardian describes the find as shedding light on the mystery, and I like the thought that the most human document of a grand scientific adventure turns out to be a love letter.

The Good News Network's history columns offer two small anniversaries that suit the same mood. Yesterday's recalled that on the thirtieth of October, nineteen seventy-three, the Bosporus Bridge was completed, linking mainland Europe with Anatolia for the first time. The piece notes its engineering, the steel towers and the inclined hangers, which is a graceful phrase in itself. A bridge between two continents is a rather poetic thing to have built, and a good image to keep in your pocket for the day. Today's column marks the birth, seventy-six years ago, of the British-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, on the thirty-first of October. It recalls her knighthood, and it notes that her London firm continues to innovate. So we have a bridge between continents yesterday and a woman who reshaped how buildings can look today, a pleasing pair for the end of the month.

Now to words, which I know are close to your heart. The Guardian reports that Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, for her book Foretokens. The collection draws on new parenthood, the death of her father, and her mother's early life in Hong Kong. The prize was announced at London's Southbank Centre, and it carries ten thousand pounds. What strikes me is the range of that subject matter: the beginning of a life, the end of one, and a mother's story from another place, all held in one book. If you're looking for contemporary poetry that moves between generations and between continents, this sounds like a very good place to start.

There's also fiction news from further afield. According to Korea Herald, via UA.NEWS, the South African novelist Damon Galgut has won the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award. I only have the headline, so I can't say more about the ceremony or the citation, but it's a welcome recognition for a Booker-winning writer, and a small sign of literature travelling well across languages and borders. Whether you've already read him or not, it's a name worth a moment of attention.

And there's something gently lyrical in the science pages this week. Good News Network reports on new research suggesting that the expertise needed to identify birds helps preserve neuroplasticity and may slow cognitive decline in ageing. The article opens with Emily Dickinson's line about hope being the thing with feathers, which seems exactly right. The finding is encouraging in a quiet way: that learning to tell one bird from another, to pay close attention to flicker and song, is good for the brain. It suggests that the habit of noticing, which is also the habit of a reader and a poet, may be a form of protection. I'll leave you to decide whether that counts as an argument for a walk along the Grésivaudan with a pair of binoculars. I rather think it does.

Also on the subject of language, Upworthy features a linguist who shows how English expressions such as "by the way" and "of course" reveal a hidden metaphor: that thinking is walking. The text I've seen is thin, so I can only give you the idea, but it's a good one. We speak of ways and courses, of getting somewhere with an argument, and without noticing, we are describing thought as a journey on foot. It could make a lovely five-minute starter for a class, asking students to spot the walking hiding in their own sentences. And there's a pleasing echo with the Bosporus Bridge, if you want to stretch the thread.

Turning to performance, there's a video from the Royal Ballet and Opera on YouTube in which the principal dancer Yasmine Naghdi talks about returning to Manon. She is back in rehearsals and on the Main Stage after maternity leave, and she speaks about what that return means. It's a gentle, human glimpse behind the curtain, a dancer coming back to a role she knows, changed by what has happened in between. Manon runs at the Royal Opera House until the twenty-fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, and a cinema broadcast ends on Tuesday the third of November, so if you wanted to see it on a screen rather than in London, the time is short. Given your fondness for dance films, it might be worth checking whether a showing is within reach.

Also on the screen, a short documentary has been drawing attention: Panther Pat, about Pat Palinkas. In nineteen seventy, she was an elementary school teacher who became the first woman to play professional football, taking the field for the Orlando Panthers. Good News Network says she has been nearly forgotten, and the film sets out to put that right. It has a strong central character, a sports-history angle, and a teacher at its heart, which I suspect you'll warm to. It's the sort of story that teaches a bit of social history without ever feeling like a lesson.

Finally, a few stories of kindness and learning, which seem to suit the last day of the month. Good News Network tells of He Ziqi, now a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence, who was admitted to a prestigious university partly because of a strawberry farmer. The farmer's phone number had appeared, without his knowing, on a middle-school English exam. He has since taken to treating the calls he receives as opportunities, using them to inspire other people. There is something wonderfully novelistic about that: a stranger's accidental part in someone else's education, and a man who responds to the interruption with generosity rather than irritation. For a teacher of English, a story in which an exam question changes a life is perhaps especially pleasing.

From Texas, a school district has named a new school after Marilyn Hampton, a longtime custodian known to everyone as Miss Marilyn. Good News Network reports that the honour moved her deeply, and there is a video of her reaction. We tend to name buildings after the powerful and the wealthy, so it's heartening to see one named for someone whose work, keeping a school clean and welcoming, is so often overlooked. Every pupil who walks through those doors will be walking into her name.

And one more, from The Optimist Daily, whose podcast for the thirtieth of October features Vivian Ho, a teenager who built a supply network where families can request goods without filling in any forms. She also sends handmade crafts that reflect each family's cultural background. I love that detail: it's help given with dignity, and with a touch of beauty and personal attention. The same episode touches on a Kenya wildlife deal, on Halloween tips across the ages, which seems fitting for today, and on energy security for electric vehicles, though I only have the outline of those.

So that's the news for today: skies and glass, letters and photographs, prizes and poems, and a handful of people doing something kind. I hope something in it keeps you company on your way down the mountain, and that your Halloween is gentle and well lit.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's the last day of October, with Halloween at the door, and this morning's France briefing has a letter-writing sailor, a few words to savour, and some news from the lycées.

Let me start with the item I think you'll enjoy most. The Guardian reports on a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse, the scientist who was lost on Louis XVI's round-the-world voyage, which set out in seventeen eighty-five. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give a personal account of the expedition. You'll know that most of what we have about great voyages comes in the form of official logs and reports, so there is something wonderful about hearing from the man himself, in the language of the heart. The Guardian describes it as shedding light on a maritime mystery, and it does read like the opening of a novel: a ship that vanished, and a lover's letters that outlived it. If you ever wanted a way into the eighteenth century for your première students, a voice like this, speaking from the deck and not from the textbook, might be just the thing. The piece is a short one, but it's worth a look.

There is some sad news from the world of the stage and screen. Franceinfo reports that the British actor Patrick Stewart died on Wednesday the twenty-eighth of October, at the age of eighty-six. Most people will know him as Captain Picard in Star Trek, or as Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men, and franceinfo carries a line from one tribute that says he played so many mythical roles. His career lasted about sixty years, across stage and screen. The word stage matters here, I think, because it was the theatre that shaped that famously resonant voice. French viewers clearly feel his loss keenly, and franceinfo describes a wave of emotion following the announcement.

Now to Halloween, which is a strange festival in France: partly imported, partly something much older. The Local France looks at why Brittany and Normandy have Samhain festivals of their own. Samhain is a festival that draws on Celtic traditions and on wider European folklore, and the piece asks how those two regions come to mark it as Halloween approaches. It's a short article, so it offers a glimpse of regional folk customs rather than a deep history, but it's a nice reminder that the pumpkins and costumes sit on top of something far older. If you are teaching anything on folklore, ghost stories or the Gothic this term, there is a ready-made hook there.

The Local's weekly column, La Belle Vie, pairs two things that don't obviously belong together: comforting French autumn food and terrifying Halloween nights. It's a light lifestyle roundup, pleasant rather than substantial, offering suggestions for Halloween outings and something warm to eat afterwards. And the Local also has a preview of six things to look forward to in France in November. It is framed against colder weather and ongoing strikes, so it is honest about the grey side of the month, but the point of the article is to find the brighter spots. I can't tell you which six are on the list, but it is a light seasonal guide that may well turn up a cultural event or a local occasion worth putting in the diary. It's the sort of article to read with a hot drink, thinking about weekends in the Grésivaudan.

On the lighter side of daily life, there is a story about teddy bears, of a sort. The Local asks why the French are going crazy for chocolate marshmallow bears. This is a cheap children's sweet, the sort of thing sold for pennies, that French pastry chefs have given a luxury makeover. One of them goes so far as to call it the new macaron. That is quite a claim, given what the macaron has become. Whether or not the bear ends up in every pâtisserie window, it's a charming little example of French pastry culture taking something humble and making it grand. If you're passing a good pâtisserie this weekend, you might look out for one.

The Local also runs a small trio of language pieces that I think you'll like, particularly with Halloween in the air. The first is the French Phrase of the Day, "des bonbons ou un sort", which is the French way of asking the trick-or-treat question. Literally, it is sweets or a spell, which has a rather nicer sound than our blunt trick or treat. The second is the French Word of the Day, casserolade. The Local teases that it is not a dish you will find at a bistro, and I will leave you to enjoy finding out what it does mean. The third is the Expression of the Day, "mauvaise langue", literally a bad tongue. The Local suggests it is a phrase you would hope never to hear applied to you. These pieces are all short, but as a teacher of English who plainly loves the texture of language, you may enjoy the idea of a bad tongue and a casserole that isn't for dinner. They might even make a good starter for a class on idiom, comparing how each language turns the body, or the kitchen, into metaphor.

Now to schools and education, where there is a good deal going on. The Guardian has an opinion piece titled four lessons the US can learn from the youth protests in France. It concerns the mouvement lycéen, which began in mid-September over conditions in public high schools and has since spread nationwide. As the title suggests, the piece is framed around what Americans might take from it rather than around the French situation itself, so it is an outsider's view and an opinion piece at that. But as a lycée teacher, you may find it interesting to see how the movement looks from abroad, and how it is being read as a story with lessons in it. I won't try to tell you what the four lessons are, since I only have the framing, but the article is there if you want to see how a French school protest becomes an international talking point.

Closely related, and relevant for students moving on from the lycée, is a fact-check from franceinfo. The Minister for Higher Education, Philippe Baptiste, has claimed that France is the least selective country for access to higher education, and the claim is based on an OECD report. Franceinfo looked at it carefully. The headline figure, that ninety-five per cent of candidates were offered a place, turns out to be accurate. But the piece says that figure hides several realities. So the number is right, and yet it does not tell the whole story of what students experience when they apply. I don't have the details of those realities, but the lesson is a familiar one: a true statistic can still give a misleading impression. It's a useful example for any class that discusses how to read evidence, and certainly useful background if your students are beginning to think about what comes after the baccalauréat.

And for students who might look further afield, there is news from The Local about opportunities across the Atlantic. On the thirty-first of October, the European Union and Canada are due to announce a new strategic alliance, one that would ease living, studying and working across the Atlantic for their citizens. The details will matter, and I don't have them yet, but for a teacher whose students may well be thinking about universities abroad, it's worth keeping an eye on. Canada has long been a popular choice for French speakers who want an English-language or bilingual education, and anything that makes the paperwork simpler will be welcome to families.

Staying with travel, here is a reassuring note. The Local reports on a new assessment of the feared summer chaos at French airports, linked to the EU's new border system, known as EES. The report finds that the chaos did not materialise. The text is brief, so I can't give you more than that, but if you have any journeys planned, whether to Britain or elsewhere, it is good to know that the dreaded queues seem not to have arrived.

Now for something cheering from further afield. HugoDécrypte has a short video showing firefighters in Indonesia celebrating the arrival of rain, after what the report calls historic wildfires. The text is only a title and a caption, so I can't tell you more than that, but the picture is a lovely one: people who have been fighting fires for a long time, finally able to stand in the rain and rejoice. It's the sort of good news from the natural world that is worth a minute of your morning.

Finally, La Mire's daily video, this time from the twenty-ninth of October. It's a round-up of French television headlines, and I'm afraid that most of it is grim. There's a train crash in Spain, and there are debates on racism. But there are two brighter items. One is a postman who delivers the post by rowing boat, which sounds like something from a children's book, and I'd love to know more about his round. The other is a segment titled Romanin, l'autre Jean Moulin. Jean Moulin is of course a name every French pupil knows, so a segment about another figure, offered as a kind of counterpart, is intriguing. I don't know the story, but it sounds like exactly the sort of history that sticks better when it's told as a human story.

That's the France round-up for today, so I hope there is a rowing postman, a bad tongue or a chocolate bear to brighten your Halloween weekend.

ScreenRant says an eight-part psychological thriller from HBO is a must-watch once again, and MovieWeb praises an eight-part mystery thriller by Harlan Coben as a perfect one-night binge. In both cases all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you the titles, the plots, or, for the Coben, which platform it is on. HBO Max is one of yours, so it may be worth a quick search if you fancy a long evening in.

Now, the dance. The Royal Ballet and Opera has been busy on YouTube, and none of this is on your usual platforms, but it is free and well worth your time. On Thursday the twenty-ninth of October, the company livestreamed World Ballet Day, with a company class and a look at how stories are made and passed from one generation to the next in the studio. The replay may still be there, and it comes in two versions: one with British Sign Language, and one with audio description. The audio-described version is a lovely way in, because someone has to put the movement into words, and that is rather close to your own craft.

In the same spirit, there is a short World Ballet Day video called Visionaries, which shows dancers in rehearsal as they prepare Visionaries: Robbins and MacMillan for the main stage. Rehearsal footage is often more moving than performance, because you see the effort before it is hidden.

Two clips go with live productions. Principal dancer Yasmine Naghdi talks about returning to rehearsals, and to the Main Stage as Manon, after maternity leave. Manon runs at the Royal Opera House until the twenty-fifth of November, and a cinema broadcast ends on Tuesday the third of November, so that one is a close deadline. Manon is also a story with a strong, tragic heroine, which I suspect you will appreciate. And then there is a clip of Naghdi with William Bracewell dancing the Apricot and Green pas de deux from Jerome Robbins's Dances at a Gathering, set to Chopin. It returns to the Main Stage in London from the ninth to the twenty-eighth of November. Chopin and Robbins together, with no plot to follow, is something close to poetry in movement.

The opera side of the same house has two videos. Last week was World Opera Day, which is also Bizet's birthday, and the Royal Opera marked it by posting the overture to Carmen. The production returns to the Main Stage from the twenty-ninth of October, and it is a lively, brassy way to hear the score. The other is an introduction to Philipp Stölzl's new production of Verdi's A Masked Ball, which is his Royal Opera debut. The teaser promises forbidden love, conspiracy and revenge, and the run is from the thirtieth of November to the eighteenth of December.

The rest of what I have for you comes from Arte, and it is a thoughtful batch.

The one I would watch first is a reportage from ARTE Regards, called À Valence, sauver les photos de l'inondation. It follows young volunteers who are restoring photographs lost in the floods of October 2024 in Valence. Over a million images are still waiting to be saved. The film is thirty minutes long and available until 2027, and it sounds like a story about memory and about what we choose to rescue, which is a theme you could easily bring into a classroom.

Close to that in spirit is an Arte documentary asking whether beauty standards are truly eternal. It traces ideas of beauty from Antiquity to today, and it points to the persistent link between beauty and power. That is cultural history of the kind you like, and it would sit well alongside a conversation about paintings and portraits. It is available until 2030, so there is no rush.

If you are in the mood for science and ethics, there are two more. Les prothèses high-tech is a documentary in French, available until the twenty-seventh of April 2027, about how advanced prostheses are changing the autonomy and the mental health of those who wear them. It follows patients, doctors and psychologists, including a man called Georg, who hopes bionic arms can help him relearn everyday movements. It weighs both the progress and the limits, which sounds like the right balance. And there is an episode of the Arte series PhantasIA, called La fabrique des émotions artificielles, on how artificial intelligence is learning to recognise, imitate and govern human emotions. It ranges from acting and neurodivergence to psychiatry and facial recognition. It is a useful one if your pupils are curious about AI and storytelling, since it asks what we mean by feeling in the first place.

Last, something gentler. An Arte Twist episode asks why cute things do us so much good, from kawaii culture to Labubu keychains. It links art, design and the search for reassurance in troubled times. It is a small cultural essay, and probably a pleasant way to end an evening.

That is all for today, Yamuna. I hope you find a quiet hour, and something worth settling into.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Saturday. It's the thirty-first of October, so Halloween, which seems a fine excuse to begin with some eerie verse.

Literary Hub has a list called "Something Wicked This Way Comes": ten poems to read this Halloween. What makes it interesting is that it steps beyond the usual Poe, Dickinson and Shelley, and gathers spooky poems from poets not normally thought of as writers of horror. A good companion for a grey autumn morning, perhaps with something hot to drink.

Staying with books, The Guardian has Philippa Gregory looking back on her apprenticeship. She read a hundred of the eighteenth century's most popular novels, and she says it was the perfect training for a writer. She also talks about coming to Dickens rather late, about Molly Keane and Elizabeth Goudge, and about why history belongs in fiction. I think that last argument will be right up your street.

The Guardian also has an interview with the Australian writer Helen Garner, whose fiction and true crime are famously unsparing. She talks about three marriages, about being called a "rotten feminist", and about finding global recognition five decades into her career. Her line is that being hated is "very bracing", and the voice that comes through sounds frank and entirely self-possessed. It may be a good one for your memorable narrators.

And for the prize-watchers, The Conversation has gathered six experts to review the 2026 Booker Prize nominees. They argue that the list is diverse enough to offer something to all sorts of readers, and the reviews have real critical substance.

Now to the world of paintings. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists believe they have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's "La Nuit étoilée". It ties a very famous canvas to astronomy, and it makes you want to go back and look at those swirling heavens again with fresh eyes.

In Cambridge, the Fitzwilliam Museum is showing an exhibition on late Victorian art and politics, featuring William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites. It runs until the third of May, and it links painting closely with writing and design. The Guardian's week in art also mentions big hair, which I take to be a reference to those pre-Raphaelite portraits.

And closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on a donation of amateur photographs entering a museum. The subjects range from the love story of an anonymous couple to a picture connected with Alfred Dreyfus. It's a lovely idea, ordinary snapshots turning into history. The article doesn't name the museum, so I can't say whether it's anywhere near you.

Now a little something for your British section, and the BFI. NPR has an interview with Kazuo Ishiguro about "Klara and the Sun" and how he approaches writing novels about the future. Since "Never Let Me Go" is on your oral exam list, it could make a very useful link for teaching. Also, the Herald and News carries an op-ed arguing that Orwell's "1984" was a warning, not an instruction manual. It's on the oral themes list, and it might serve as a prompt for discussing what the novel is actually for.

Now, around Grenoble. On Wednesday the fourth of November, MC2 hosts "Le Sommet des dieux", a ciné-concert with Patrick Imbert. The Orchestre national Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes plays live under the conductor Jean Deroyer, so a film and an orchestra together. Also on the fourth, and again on the fifth, MC2 presents Betty Tchomanga's dance piece "The Sea is History". The listing is brief, but it is contemporary dance, so it may be worth a look. Two evenings at MC2 in the same week is a pleasing prospect.

If you'd rather stay at home, there are two things to watch. The Royal Ballet and Opera has a video of the principal dancer Yasmine Naghdi talking about coming back to rehearsals, and to the Main Stage as Manon, after maternity leave. Manon runs at the Royal Opera House until the twenty-fifth of November, and there's a cinema broadcast, which ends on Tuesday the third of November. And ARTE has a documentary, available until twenty thirty, asking whether beauty standards are eternal. It traces ideas of beauty from Antiquity to today, and notes the persistent link between beauty and power.

Time for some good news. Good News Network tells the story of He Ziqi, now a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence, who was admitted to a prestigious university partly thanks to a strawberry farmer. The farmer's phone number had appeared on a middle-school English exam, without his knowing. He now uses the calls he gets as chances to inspire people. And the same site marks today as the anniversary of the birth of the British-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, seventy-six years ago. It recalls her knighthood and her London firm, which continues to innovate.

Finally, two small pleasures from The Local France. The word of the day is "casserolade", introduced with the warning that it is not a dish you'll find at a bistro. And the expression of the day is "mauvaise langue", which is a phrase you would hope never to hear applied to yourself.

That's your Daily Yam for today, Yamuna. I hope your Saturday is full of good pages and good light over Belledonne.
